title: The number is not the money.
dek: Ann got a 2% raise with no inflation, Barbara got 5% with 4% inflation. 71% of people knew Ann was richer, 64% still thought Barbara was happier. My savings fool me the same way.
whyThisIdea: The backlog has only ideas already marked too close to published posts, so this is a new one for Black Friday week: money illusion (Shafir, Diamond & Tversky 1997), the real value of savings, with the arithmetic in the open - money and psychology, the core of your territory, and a natural follow-up to your Psychology of Money review, which never asked what the money would buy.

entry.title: The number is not the money.
entry.titleHtml: The number is not the money.
entry.dek: Ann got a 2% raise with no inflation, Barbara got 5% with 4% inflation. 71% of people knew Ann was richer, 64% still thought Barbara was happier. My savings fool me the same way.
body: “A bigger number is not always more money.”

Have you ever asked yourself if €1.000 is still €1.000 ten years later? It sounds like a stupid question. The note is the same, the number on it is the same, nobody took anything from you. Today is Monday, the 23rd of November, and this is the week when everybody looks at prices more than at any other time of the year. But there is one price nobody looks at, and it is the price of money itself. So the question is: if the number in your account never goes down, can you still be getting poorer? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at has a name, money illusion, and I met it while reading about inflation, after I wrote my review of “The Psychology of Money”. In that review I did all the maths about compound interest - Warren Buffett, 22%, $25.000 at 10 years old - and I never once asked what the money would actually buy at the end. In 1997, three researchers, Eldar Shafir, Peter Diamond and Amos Tversky, published a paper in the Quarterly Journal of Economics that described exactly this mistake: the tendency to think about money in its nominal value, the number, instead of its real value, what it can buy.

Firstly, let’s split the idea in two, the way I like to do. “The number” and “the money”. The number is what is written on the note, on the screen, on the payslip. It is very easy to see and very easy to compare - 31.500 is bigger than 30.600, done. The money is something else. It is how many coffees, books, train tickets or months of rent that number turns into. And the money is invisible, because to see it you need to know what happened to thousands of prices at the same time. <u>We remember the number because it is written down. The money we have to calculate, so most of the time we don’t.</u>

Secondly, let’s look at the experiment, because it is very simple and I almost failed it myself. The researchers told people a story about two women, Ann and Barbara, who finished the same college a year apart and both started with a salary of $30.000. In Ann’s first year there was no inflation, and she got a raise of 2%. In Barbara’s first year prices went up by 4%, and she got a raise of 5%. Let’s do the arithmetic:
Ann: $30.000 + 2% = $30.600, and prices did not move
Barbara: $30.000 + 5% = $31.500, but everything costs 4% more, so in old prices it is $31.500 ÷ 1.04 = $30.288
So Barbara has the bigger number, but Ann has the bigger salary. Barbara’s real raise is 1.05 ÷ 1.04 = less than 1%, about half of Ann’s.

And here is the part that surprised me. When people were asked who was better off in economic terms, about 71% said Ann, which is correct. Most people can do the maths when you ask them to. But when they were asked who was happier at her job, 64% said Barbara. The same people who knew Ann was richer still believed Barbara felt better. And I think they were right about the feeling, which is exactly the problem. A 5% raise feels like a 5% raise, even when half of it was eaten before it arrived.

Now let’s bring it closer to home, because I do not have a salary, but I do have savings. Let’s say I put €1.000 in a drawer and leave it there for ten years, and prices go up by 2% every year, which is the target of the European Central Bank, so not a crazy number. After ten years the note still says €1.000, but it buys what €820 buys today:
€1.000 ÷ 1.0210 = €820.35
And 2% is the calm version. In October 2022, prices in the euro area were 10.6% higher than a year before. At that speed, the same €1.000 loses almost €96 of what it can buy in a single year: €1.000 ÷ 1.106 = €904.16.

The bank account is the most interesting case, because it gives you a feeling of winning. Let’s say the account pays 1% a year and prices go up by 2%. After ten years the screen shows €1.104 (and 62 cents) - more than you put in, very satisfying. But in today’s prices that is worth €906.17. So the screen says you won about €105, and in reality you lost about €94 (yes, you read that right, both at the same time). Money that does not move is not standing still. It is going backwards slowly enough that you never notice.

Thirdly, I have to be fair to the other side, because the solution is not as simple as “never keep cash”. To beat inflation you have to put the money somewhere where it can grow, and everything that can grow can also fall. I wrote about this in my article on nothing to lose and nothing to spare - a bet can be good on average and still hurt the person who cannot afford the loss. Money in a drawer or in a normal account is also the money that is there when the laptop breaks or the bus pass needs to be paid. Losing 2% a year on that is not a mistake. It is the price of being able to sleep, and sometimes it is a fair price. The mistake is only not knowing that you are paying it.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. From now on, every time I compare a number from the past with a number from today - my savings, a price, a salary somebody tells me about - I will ask one extra question: not “how much is it?”, but “what does it buy?”. And once a year, in November, I will write down what my savings could buy then and what they can buy now, not just the number.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I think money illusion is one of the quietest mistakes there is, exactly because nothing in your life tells you it is happening - no message, no red number, nothing. But I have to be honest about two things. My examples use one inflation rate for everything, and real life does not work like that - for a student, the price of food and transport matters much more than the average of all prices, and my own inflation can be higher or lower than the official one. And thinking in real money all the time is exhausting. If I divided every price by 1.02<sup>years</sup> before buying a coffee, I would never enjoy anything. What I take from it is smaller: when the number goes up, check if the money went up too.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“A bigger number is not always more money.”
